This criminal revision petition u/s 438 of BNSS, 2023 has been filed by the revisionist against the order dated 23.10.2024 passed by the court of Ms. Chhavi Bansal, Ld. JMFC-11, South East District,
Saket Courts, New Delhi, in complaint case No. 2060/2023 titled as "Pawan Kaul Vs. Ram Kishan Koli" vide which application u/s.156(3) Cr.PC filed by the revisionist was dismissed.

sentences.text: 2. By filing the present revision petition, revisionist seeks to set aside the impugned dismissal order of the application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C dated 23.10.2024 passed by the Ld. Trial Court.

3. Brief facts of the case, as stated in the revision petition, are that marriage between revisionist and respondent no.4 was solemnized on 02.03.2014 and after few days respondent no.4 started misbehaving and harassing the revisionist by misusing the position of her father i.e. respondent no.2, who was working in CBI and has now retired, and filed a false and frivolous case against the revisionist and his family u/s 498A IPC and all the respondents made the life of the revisionist miserable.

On 08.09.2017, the father of the revisionist was forcefully pushed behind a standing truck by a goon and another goon who was present at the spot took out a pistol and pointed the same at the father of the revisionist and demanded Rs. 20 lakhs and father of revisionist lodged a detailed complaint which was recorded vide DD No.37B dated 30.09.2027 at PS Samaypur Badli,
Delhi.

All the respondents were aware that the revisionist never worked at M/S Lakshay - The Target educational society, yet they made defamatory allegations to the employer of the revisionist that the revisionist was working as a tally teacher at the society and this act of giving false information adversely impacted the reputation of the revisionist at his work place.
The respondents gave wrong phone numbers of the revisionist to DDA/the employer of the revisionist.
The revisionist gave a complaint to SHO PS Kotla Mubarkapur, ACP Defence Colony and DCP South district but no action was taken.
Thus, revisionist filed a complaint u/s. 200 Cr.PC alongwith an application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C before Ld. Trial Court for registration of FIR.

4. Action taken report filed by the police before Ld. Trial Court perused in which it is mentioned that the incident took place at Samaypur Badli on 08.09.2017 and the matter was reported in PS Samaypur Badli vide GD No.37B dated 30.09.2017 and no cognizable offence was found to be made out in the jurisdiction of PS K. M. Pur.

1 5.
Ld. Trial Court dismissed the application u/s.156(3) Cr.PC after observing that there is prior background of matrimonial dispute between the parties.
As per the ATR, the alleged incident of 08.09.2017 took place in the jurisdiction of PS Samaypur Badli.
Defamation is not cognizable offence.
The identity of the accused is not disputed and is in the knowledge of the complainant and there appears no requirement of custodial interrogation of the accused.
All incriminating facts are already in the knowledge of the complainant and there are no facts left to be unearthed which may require investigation by the police.

6. Impugned order is challenged on the ground that Ld. Trial Court failed to consider the gravity of offences of criminal intimidation (Sec 506 IPC), extortion (Sec.384 IPC) and provision of false information to a public servant (Sec.182 IPC), which necessitate immediate police investigation.
7. Case file alongwith TCR and documents perused.
8. The allegations regarding the manhandling of the father of revisionist took place in the area of PS Samaypur Badli which lies in North District and not in the jurisdiction of Ld. Trial Court.

Another allegation is made regarding filing of false case u/s. 498A IPC but during arguments it was admitted that Trial in the case is still going on, so, without the conclusion of the trial it cannot be said whether a false case was filed or not.
And even if, false case has been filed then the remedy is damages for malicious prosecution and not the registration of FIR.
9. Another allegation made regarding the defamation which is not a cognizable offence.

During arguments, counsel for the revisionist submits that documents containing wrong / false information qua the revisionist were filed by the respondents in his employer's office i.e. DDA and to recover those documents police investigation is required.
The alleged documents can be summoned by the court on appropriate application moved by the revisionist during recording of his evidence u/s. 223 BNSS.
Therefore, no police investigation is required.

10. Few of the judgments in which directions to be followed while deciding application u/s. 156(3)
Cr.PC given by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi are discussed hereinbelow :

In "M/s Skipper Beverages Pvt. Ltd. v State", 2001(2) JCC (Delhi) 67, the Hon'ble High Court has observed as under:
"It is true that Section 156(3) of the Code empowers to Magistrate to direct the police to register a case and intimate investigations but this power has to be exercised judiciously on proper grounds and not in a mechanical manner.

entities.text: M/s Skipper Beverages Pvt. Ltd. v State", 2001(2) JCC (Delhi) 67
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In those cases where the allegations are not very serious and the complainant himself is in possession of evidence to prove his allegations there should be no need to pass orders under Section 156(3) of the Code.

This discretion ought to be exercised after proper application of mind and only in those cases where the Magistrate is of the view that the nature of the allegations is such that the complainant himself may not be in a position to collect and produce evidence before the court and interest of justice demand that the police should step in the help of the complainant."

In "V. P. Sharma (Dr.) v State (NCT of Delhi) & Ors", 2009 XAD (Delhi) 701, the Hon'ble High Court has observed as under:
"The insistence to direct the Magistrate to take the other course of exercise of directing registration of FIR by calling for an investigation under Section 156(3) CrPC is putting the entire CrPC on a different pedestal.

entities.text: V. P. Sharma (Dr.) v State (NCT of Delhi) & Ors", 2009 XAD (Delhi) 701
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is being raised by people who does not want to lead evidence or who does not have evidence to substantiate the complaint in accordance with law.
In the present case also, the petitioner has not chosen to file a complaint under Section 200 CrPC and he wanted to adopt a shortcut.
More so, when the allegation prima facie reveals that it is a civil matter."
Also in "Subh Karan Luharuka & Anr. Vs. State & Anr.", 2010(3) JCC 1972.

entities.text: Subh Karan Luharuka & Anr. Vs. State & Anr.", 2010(3) JCC 1972
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Those guidelines are as under.

"52A. For the guidance of subordinate Courts, the procedure to be followed while dealing with an application u/s 156 (3) of the Code is summarized as under:
1.

Whenever a Magistrate is called upon to pass orders u/s 153(3) of the code, at the outset, the Magistrate should ensure that before coming to the Court, the complainant did approach the police officer in charge of the Police of Station having jurisdiction over the area for recording the information available with him disclosing the commission of a cognizable offence by the persons/persons arrayed as an accused in the complainant.
It should also be examined as to what action was taken by the SHO, or even by the senior officer of the Police, when approached by the complainant u/s 154 (3) of the Code.

2. The Magistrate should then form his own opinion whether the facts mentioned in the complainant disclose commission of cognizable offence by the accused persons arrayed in the complainant which can be tried in his jurisdiction.
He should also satisfy himself about the need for investigation by the police in the matter.
A preliminary inquiry as this is permissible even by an SHO and if no such inquiry has been done by the SHO, then it is all the more necessary for the Magistrate to consider all these factors.
For that purpose, the Magistrate must apply his mind and such application of mind should be reflected in the Order passed by him.

Upon a preliminary satisfaction, unless there are exceptional circumstances to be recorded in writing, a status report by the police is to be called for before passing final orders.
3. The Magistrate when approached with a Complaint u/s 200 of the Code, should invariably proceed under Chapter XV by taking cognizance of the Complaint, recording evidence and then deciding the question of issuance of process to the accused.
In that case also, the Magistrate is fully entitled to postpone the process if it is felt that there is a necessity to call for a police report u/s 202 of the Code.

sentences.text: Of course, it is open to the Magistrate to proceed under Chapter XII of the code when an application u/s 156(3) of the Code is also filed along with a complaint u/s 200 of the Code if the Magistrate decides not to take cognizance of the Complaint.

However in that case, the Magistrate,
before passing any order to proceed under Chapter XII , should not only satisfy himself about the pre-requisites as aforesaid, but, additionally, he should also be satisfied that it is necessary to direct Police investigation in the matter for collection of evidence which is neither in the possession of the complainant nor can be produced by the witnesses on being summoned by the Court at the instance complainant, and the matter is such which calls for investigation by a State agency.

The Magistrate must pass an order giving cogent reasons as to why he intends to proceed under Chapter XII instead of Chapter XV of the Code."
11.

As per the clear cut guidelines issued by our Hon'ble High Court as extracted above, it is the Paramount duty of the Court to satisfy itself when the case is such a nature where it is necessary to direct police investigation in the matter for collection of evidence which was neither in possession of the complainant nor could be produced by the witness of the complainant and the matter was,
therefore, of such a nature which called for investigation by the investigating agency.
But in the present case, as discussed above, all the witnesses are known to the complainant and evidence are within his reach.
Therefore, Ld. Trial Court has passed the order complying with the directions given in the above-mentioned judgments.

12. Further, it is to be kept in mind that revision jurisdiction is normally to be exercised in exceptional cases where there is a glaring defect in procedure or there is manifest error of law and consequently there has been a flagrant miscarriage of justice.
The order passed by Ld. JMFC is a speaking order.

If impugned order is analyzed in light of scope of section 438/440 BNSS, no wrong,
illegality, impropriety or irregularity is noticed therein.
13. Accordingly, in view of the above observations, the present revision petition is dismissed.
There is no illegality and infirmity in the order dated 23.10.2024 passed by Ld. Trial Court.
Ld. Trial Court is directed to proceed further as per law.
14. TCR alongwith copy of this order be sent back to the concerned Learned Trial Court.
15. Revision file be consigned to the Record Room after due compliance.
